title: China tears up Meta's AI deal, and it was already done
subtitle: China blocked Meta's $2 billion acquisition of Manus and ordered both sides to unwind a transaction that was already complete.
author: Thorium Valley
content:
China just killed a deal that was already closed.

On Monday, China's National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC) blocked Meta's $2 billion acquisition of Manus, the Chinese-founded AI agent startup, and ordered both sides to unwind the transaction entirely. The acquisition had largely been completed. China decided it didn't care.

The NDRC said the decision was made "in accordance with laws and regulations" and required the parties to withdraw the acquisition. Meta pushed back, with a spokesperson issuing a public statement that "the transaction complied fully with applicable law" and that the company anticipates "an appropriate resolution to the inquiry."

The block follows what was widely reported as a months-long probe into the deal. But the timing tells a bigger story. This isn't China screening a proposed deal before it closes, which is standard practice globally. This is China reaching backward to rip up something that already happened. That's a very different kind of move.

Manus had become one of the hottest AI agent startups in the world, reportedly hitting a $125 million annual revenue run rate and drawing attention from Silicon Valley's biggest players. For Meta, the acquisition was a bet on the booming AI agent space, where tools like OpenClaw and Claude Cowork are reshaping how people and companies get work done. Manus, with its roots in China and its growing global customer base, looked like a strategic win.

But that's also what made it a target. A BCG analysis on foreign investment found that governments are increasingly tightening their oversight of inbound and outbound investment in strategic sectors like semiconductors and critical minerals to protect economic security. The traditional foreign investment playbook, where regulators screen inbound deals before they close, is being rewritten in real time. China's move against Meta goes further than any of those precedents.

The decision also lands in the middle of an intensifying US-China tech split. The US has been tightening export controls to keep advanced AI chips and capabilities out of Chinese hands. China blocking an American company from acquiring Chinese AI talent is the mirror image of that same instinct. Both sides are now actively preventing the other from accessing what they consider strategic AI resources.

The ripple effects could be immediate. A growing number of Chinese-founded AI startups have redomiciled to Singapore, the US, and other jurisdictions in recent years, partly to access global capital and partly to sidestep exactly this kind of regulatory risk. If China is willing to retroactively unwind completed deals, that calculus gets a lot more urgent for founders who still have any operational ties to the mainland.

Meta, for its part, has options. It can challenge the decision, negotiate, or walk away. But even if this particular deal gets resolved, the precedent is set.

The NDRC didn't just block a deal. It established that no cross-border AI acquisition involving Chinese-founded companies is truly final until Beijing says it is. For every American tech company eyeing AI talent or startups with roots in China, that's a new risk factor that didn't exist six months ago. And for Chinese-founded startups trying to raise money or sell to Western buyers, the message from their own government is clear: your cap table is a national security question now. The founders who saw this coming already moved. The ones who didn't just watched their exit options narrow considerably.

title: Musk v. Altman finally goes to court
subtitle: The most expensive grudge match in tech history starts today. Whether it changes anything is a different question.
author: Thorium Valley
content:
The most expensive grudge match in tech history starts today. Whether it changes anything is a different question.

Elon Musk's lawsuit against Sam Altman and OpenAI goes to trial Monday in Oakland, with Musk seeking up to $134.5 billion in damages. Jury selection begins in front of Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers, the same judge who presided over Apple v. Epic Games, and the witness list includes Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati.

The core of Musk's case is straightforward. He co-founded OpenAI in 2015 as a nonprofit dedicated to building AI "for the benefit of humanity." Since then, OpenAI has restructured into a for-profit entity, raised $122 billion, and hit a valuation north of $850 billion. Musk says that transformation betrayed everything he helped build. His lawyers have described the situation as "perfidy and deceit of Shakespearean proportions."

Before the trial started, Musk voluntarily dropped his fraud claims, narrowing the case to breach of charitable trust and unjust enrichment. Fraud is harder to prove and carries harsher consequences. By stripping those claims out, Musk is betting on a cleaner story for the jury: OpenAI made promises, then it broke them.

OpenAI has a very different version of events. In a blog post titled "The truth Elon left out," the company argues that Musk himself pushed for OpenAI to become a for-profit entity and wanted majority equity and full control. One of the more revealing details from the filings: Musk reportedly said he "wanted to accumulate $80 billion for a self-sustaining city on Mars" and that he needed and deserved majority ownership to make that happen. OpenAI has called the entire lawsuit a "broader strategy of harassment aimed at slowing us down and advantaging his own AI company, xAI."

The trial is happening in the Bay Area, where practically everyone has strong feelings about AI, tech billionaires, or both. Elizabeth Lippy, director of trial advocacy at Temple University's law school, told CNN that "the law doesn't require jurors who have never heard of Elon Musk or AI. It requires jurors who can put aside what they've heard and decide the case based only on the evidence presented in court."

The trial could stretch several weeks. But the more interesting question is whether the verdict matters as much as the lawsuit itself. Musk's case has already forced OpenAI to publicly defend its corporate transformation at every step, kept the debate over its founding mission alive for years, and injected legal uncertainty into every fundraise and partnership the company has pursued. OpenAI restructured its Microsoft partnership just this week to resolve complications tied to its $50 billion Amazon deal, exactly the kind of ongoing corporate maneuvering that sits at the heart of what Musk is complaining about.

A $134.5 billion verdict would obviously matter. But Musk's real leverage was never the courtroom. His lawsuit turned OpenAI's founding documents into a public liability, forced the company to explain itself on repeat, and gave every competitor and regulator a convenient narrative to point to whenever OpenAI's mission comes up. Win or lose, Musk proved that what you promise when you start an AI company can haunt you for a very long time. Every AI founder watching this trial should be reading their own incorporation papers tonight.

title: OpenAI is designing a phone chip to challenge the iPhone
subtitle: OpenAI is taking a shot at the smartphone with a custom processor targeting 300 to 400 million units a year.
author: Thorium Valley
content:
OpenAI is taking a shot at the smartphone.

Apple analyst Ming-Chi Kuo reported on Monday that OpenAI is working with Qualcomm and MediaTek to develop a custom smartphone processor, with Luxshare as the manufacturing partner. Mass production is targeted for 2028, though Kuo noted that specs and suppliers won't be finalized until late 2026 or early 2027.

The production target is what stands out: 300 to 400 million units annually. Apple shipped roughly 230 million iPhones last year. OpenAI is planning for volume that would match or exceed the most popular consumer device on the planet.

Qualcomm stock jumped 12% on the report. CEO Cristiano Amon has said that a recent drop in quarterly guidance was "100% related to memory" constraints, as suppliers diverted production to AI data centers, causing a shortage of smartphone DRAM.

That local capability matters because of what this phone is supposed to do. The concept, according to Ming-Chi Kuo, is built around AI agents replacing traditional apps entirely. Instead of opening one app for food delivery, another for your calendar, another for flights, you'd just tell ChatGPT what you need and agents would handle the rest. Research on running AI at the edge shows that mobile processors currently suffer from severe thermal throttling under sustained load, which highlights the need for highly specialized, dedicated silicon.

That said, this is one analyst's report about a product that is two years out. Altman posted on X that it "feels like a good time to seriously rethink how operating systems and user interfaces are designed," but hasn't announced a phone. We've covered OpenAI prototyping everything from earbuds to smart lamps, and companies routinely float reports like these to gauge public interest before committing to build anything. OpenAI also isn't the only AI company reaching for custom silicon. As we reported Wednesday, Google unveiled its own custom AI chips, part of a broader instinct across the industry that if your software demands specialized hardware, eventually you design your own.

That 300 to 400 million unit target isn't a phone. It's a platform. OpenAI is almost certainly thinking about licensing a chip to multiple device manufacturers, the way Qualcomm's Snapdragon already powers most of the Android world. Building a single device that competes with the iPhone means taking on Apple's supply chains, its app ecosystem, and a level of consumer trust that took a decade and hundreds of billions of dollars to earn. Licensing an "AI-first" chip to hardware partners would let OpenAI do what it actually does best: build the software, not the phone.

title: Two employees. $1.8B in sales. All AI.
subtitle: A two-person telehealth startup sold $400 million in weight-loss drugs in its first year using AI for everything. Then journalists started checking the doctors.
author: Thorium Valley
content:
Matthew Gallagher spent $20,000 and two months building a telehealth company that sold $401 million worth of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs in its first year. He used AI to write the code, generate ad creatives, handle customer service, and analyze business performance. His only employee is his brother Elliot. The New York Times ran a glowing profile on April 2 calling Medvi a case study in what AI makes possible, with Gallagher on track for $1.8 billion in 2026 sales.

The problem is that the FDA had already sent Medvi a warning letter six weeks earlier.

The letter, dated Feb. 20, flagged Medvi for misbranding violations. The company's website falsely suggested Medvi was the compounder of its semaglutide and tirzepatide products and made claims like "Same active ingredient as Wegovy®" that regulators said were misleading. None of this appeared in the Times profile.

Then investigations by Business Insider and Drug Discovery & Development started checking the doctors.

As of their investigations, at least six purported doctor pages were marketing Medvi's weight-loss and erectile dysfunction products. "Dr. Matthew Anderson MD" listed an Angolan phone number and appeared to have previously belonged to a gospel musician. Ads ran under names including "Professor Albust Dongledore" and "Dr. Richard Hörzgock," using AI-generated video testimonials and recycled identical scripts across multiple fabricated personas. One Facebook page for a "Dr. Robert Whitworth" was categorized as a Congolese clothing store.

On Friday, more than 5,000 active ad campaigns mentioning or linking to Medvi were live on Meta. By Monday, after Business Insider drew Gallagher's attention to profiles with signs of AI use including Gemini watermarks, that number fell to roughly 2,800.

Gallagher told Business Insider that the company has a clear policy of providing disclosure on any AI portrayal of a doctor, and that "if we find an affiliate doing this we work to take these ads" down. He blamed rogue affiliates for the fake profiles. But as the National Consumers League petition to the FTC put it: what telehealth platforms like Medvi are doing exposes consumers to unsubstantiated claims and violates the FTC's prohibition against false and deceptive advertising.

The regulatory exposure runs deeper than the ads. Medvi was one of six telehealth companies named in a request for an FTC investigation sent in September by the National Consumers League and other organizations, months before the Times profile ran. The company has also been sued at least twice in the past 11 months by people claiming Medvi and its affiliate marketers violated spam laws by sending unsolicited texts and emails. And OpenLoop Health, the clinical infrastructure partner that Medvi relies on, disclosed a January 2026 cybersecurity breach in which a threat actor claimed to have exfiltrated records from approximately 1.6 million patients.

It's also worth noting that the $1.8 billion figure in every headline is a revenue projection, not a valuation. The Times itself buried the fact that Medvi has not raised outside funding and has no official valuation. A company's value is typically established by investors, an acquisition offer, or public market pricing. Medvi has none of those.

Gallagher's response to the scrutiny has been revealing. In a now-deleted post on X, he called his critics "the most low t guys" and "the Karens of the internet." In another post he compared the backlash to cavemen discovering fire, writing that "white label telemedicine is a huge benefit with a net positive." Dr. Jonathan Slotkin, a neurosurgeon and hospital executive, told Futurism the Times profile read like "a transcript of a Silicon Valley fever dream" and that "it probably needed to be reported as a health story, with the same questions that are asked in health stories. It didn't look like a health story to me; it looked like a tech story."

That framing problem is the whole thing. AI made it possible for one person to build an ad machine that generated hundreds of millions in revenue selling prescription medication. The same AI tools that wrote Medvi's code and produced its marketing also generated fake doctor profiles convincing enough that nobody caught them until a second newsroom actually Googled the names. Gary Marcus, cognitive scientist and longtime AI critic, called the Times profile "not The New York Times' finest hour" and a "warning sign for how AI can be abused."

Into the Valley

The Medvi story is going to become a reference point for a very specific kind of failure, not AI hallucination, where a model makes something up by accident, but AI-manufactured legitimacy, where someone uses these tools to build an entire trust apparatus that looks real from every angle until you check. Five thousand ad campaigns. LegitScript certification. A founder profile in the paper of record. Everything worked exactly as designed, and the only thing that caught it was a journalist who bothered to look up whether the doctors were real people. As AI tools get cheaper and faster, the gap between "I automated my business" and "I automated deception at scale" is going to keep shrinking. The question for regulators is whether they can close that gap before the next Medvi gets even bigger.

title: Verizon spent $1,538 per worker to prepare for AI
subtitle: A CEO who cut 13,000 jobs, set aside $20 million to reskill them, and then went on a media tour warning unemployment could hit 30%.
author: Thorium Valley
content:
Dan Schulman became Verizon's CEO last October and within a month cut more than 13,000 positions, roughly 20% of the company's nonunion workforce. He simultaneously announced a $20 million reskilling fund to prepare those workers for what he called the "age of AI." That fund, divided evenly, comes out to about $1,538 per person.

By April, Schulman was on a full media tour. He told the Wall Street Journal that AI and humanoid robots would push unemployment to 20% to 30% within two to five years. He compared the technology's significance to the Renaissance and the invention of fire. He urged fellow CEOs to stop sugarcoating what's coming for their employees.

"It's a very difficult time, and everyone knows it is," Schulman said. "So I think being authentic, being realistic, telling the truth, as best you can, is essential."

That authenticity extended to specifics. At a Morgan Stanley conference in March, Schulman didn't mince words about the cuts going beyond the initial 13,000. "We took out a whole heck of a lot of our contracted workforce as well," he said. Verizon also started converting 179 corporate stores to franchises and reviewing its office space across four states. Then the company went quiet. Fierce Network noted that Verizon had gone unusually silent on specifics while the restructuring continued internally.

What Schulman doesn't bring up in those interviews is that Verizon was shrinking long before generative AI existed. Between 2015 and October 2022, the company saw its headcount fall by 58,200 employees. In 2016, Verizon had about 161,000 workers and operating costs around $97 billion. By last year, headcount was under 90,000 and those costs had actually climbed to roughly $109 billion. A decade of layoffs and the bills still went up.

The business pressures tell a clearer story than the AI rhetoric. Verizon lost about 2.25 million customers over the past three years because of price hikes and tougher competition. Postpaid phone churn reached 0.95% in the fourth quarter of 2025, up 7 basis points from the same quarter the year prior. This is a telecom company dealing with telecom problems, and AI provides a much better narrative for cuts that were already in motion.

Schulman's own 30% unemployment prediction also creates a problem for his bottom line if you follow it to its logical end. Verizon's postpaid wireless business averages almost $150 a month per account. If nearly a third of Americans are out of work, millions of those customers simply can't afford that bill anymore. For context, 30% unemployment would be several points worse than the Great Depression.

Wall Street hasn't rallied behind the vision either. Verizon's stock is down roughly 20% since 2021, though the shares are still worth a bit more than when Schulman took over. Light Reading started calling him "telecom's AI doomster-in-chief."

Into the Valley

Schulman might be the most candid CEO in corporate America right now, and there is something genuinely refreshing about a leader who warns employees before cutting them rather than after. But candor and investment are two very different things, and $1,538 per worker is a rounding error with a press release attached to it. Verizon was cutting tens of thousands of jobs for a decade before anyone had heard of ChatGPT. The new CEO just found better language for it.

title: Duolingo graded employees on AI use. They graded back.
subtitle: The CEO told employees AI use would factor into performance reviews. They had one question he couldn't answer.
author: Thorium Valley
content:
Luis von Ahn told every Duolingo employee that AI use would factor into their performance reviews. Their response, as he put it on a recent podcast, was a question he couldn't really answer: "Do you just want us to use AI for AI's sake?"

On the April 10 episode of the Silicon Valley Girl podcast, the Duolingo CEO confirmed the company had fully reversed course. "At the end, we backtracked, and we said, 'No, look. The most important thing in your performance is you are doing whatever your job is as well as possible,'" von Ahn said. "A lot of times AI can help you with that, but if it can't, I'm not going to force you to do that."

The original announcement wasn't an internal memo that leaked. Von Ahn posted it to Duolingo's LinkedIn on April 28, 2025, comparing the moment to the company's bet on mobile back in 2013. "AI is already changing how work gets done," he wrote. "We are making a similar call now." The strategy included what he called "constructive constraints," meaning AI use would be tracked in reviews, AI proficiency would factor into hiring, and contractors would gradually be phased out for work that AI could handle.

It was a public performance as much as a corporate strategy, and the public responded accordingly. Von Ahn was back on LinkedIn within weeks admitting the rollout hadn't gone well. He clarified that the company was still hiring at the same speed and that he didn't see AI replacing what employees do. By August he was telling the New York Times, "This was on me. I did not give enough context."

Not everything got walked back, though. Duolingo had already cut 10% of its contract workforce at the end of 2023, with some of those layoffs tied directly to AI replacing content generation tasks. Even after the performance review reversal, the contractor pause remains in place.

Von Ahn's explanation for why the review metric failed is the most useful part of this whole saga. "It felt like, rather than being held accountable for the actual outcome, we were trying to push something that in some cases did not fit," he said. And he was specific about where it broke: "The reality is it's not yet the case that AI is better at coding than a human. Therefore, if I make an engineer and say, 'You will be evaluated on how much AI you use,' it doesn't make sense."

When you track whether someone used the tool instead of whether the work got better, people optimize for the metric. Duolingo's employees figured that out immediately. The company eventually replaced the mandate with "F-r-A-I-days", a dedicated block of time for people to experiment with AI tools on their own terms rather than getting graded on it.

Duolingo isn't the only company wrestling with this. Meta has set goals for how much some employees should use AI tools. Non-technical Google employees have been told that AI use is expected and could show up in reviews. The pressure to demonstrate AI fluency has gotten intense enough that Forbes is writing about "AI-maxxing", the growing workplace trend of conspicuously using AI tools to signal competence, and the fact that it's getting on everybody's nerves.

Von Ahn's AI-first strategy eventually landed in the Museum of Failure under the category "AI Failure Corporate." That's a pretty definitive performance review.

Into the Valley

The temptation to measure AI adoption through HR metrics is going to hit every organization sooner or later because grading tool usage feels concrete in a way that "foster a culture of experimentation" does not. But von Ahn just ran the experiment for the rest of the business world, and the result was clear. title: The AI rivalry that's now everyone's problem
subtitle: OpenAI and Anthropic are in an open fight over what AI should be used for. The consequences are showing up everywhere.
author: Thorium Valley
content:
OpenAI and Anthropic are in an open fight over what AI should be used for. The consequences are showing up everywhere.

OpenAI signed a deal with the Department of War earlier this year to provide its models for classified military systems. Anthropic was offered similar terms and walked away.

CEO Dario Amodei said the company had two non-negotiable red lines: no fully autonomous weapons and no mass domestic surveillance. "Our only concerns have been our exceptions on fully autonomous weapons and mass domestic surveillance, which relate to high-level usage areas, and not operational decision-making," he wrote. Amodei also apologized to staff after an internal post about the situation leaked to the press, saying Anthropic didn't leak it and it wasn't in the company's interest for it to go public.

OpenAI's response was unusually pointed. In a FAQ on its blog, the company wrote: "We don't know why Anthropic could not reach this deal, and we hope that they and more labs will consider it." It also claimed its agreement has "more guardrails than any previous agreement for classified AI deployments, including Anthropic's." When asked whether Anthropic deserved to be designated a "supply chain risk" (Pentagon language for being blacklisted from defense work), OpenAI said no, adding it had "made our position on this clear to the government."

That a company had to publicly push back against blacklisting its biggest rival tells you how charged this has gotten.

The Pentagon disagreement is the most visible crack in a deeper split. These two companies are now building their businesses around fundamentally different theories of what wins in AI.

OpenAI is chasing revenue from every direction: government contracts, ads in ChatGPT, a $122 billion fundraise. Anthropic is betting that trust is the product. It poured $100 million into its Claude Partner Network this year, with Accenture training 30,000 professionals on Claude and Cognizant opening access across roughly 350,000 associates.

And people are picking sides. After the Pentagon deal, more than 2.5 million users reportedly removed ChatGPT or cancelled subscriptions in what became the QuitGPT movement. Claude hit No. 1 on the US App Store for the first time, with downloads jumping 240% month over month according to Appfigures data.

Enterprise spending tells a similar story. Ramp data shows Anthropic's share of enterprise customers jumped from 24.4% in March to 30.6% in April, while OpenAI dropped to 35.2%. At that pace, Anthropic could overtake OpenAI in enterprise adoption within months.

For anyone choosing between these platforms, the decision now carries real weight. Research shows 81% of leaders are already concerned about AI vendor dependency, and only 6% say they could switch providers without significant disruption. Picking a chatbot used to be about which one gave better answers. Now it's a lock-in decision.

Into the Valley

Both sides have a point, which is what makes this uncomfortable for everyone else. OpenAI says engaging directly with the military, guardrails in the contract, beats the alternative of the government building AI tools without proper oversight. Anthropic says some uses are off the table regardless. Right now the market is rewarding Anthropic for drawing lines. That only holds as long as saying "no" keeps winning customers instead of losing them.

title: Jensen Huang says AI won't take your job. Your coworker will.
subtitle: Jensen Huang doesn't think AI is coming for your job. He thinks your coworker is.
author: Thorium Valley
content:
Jensen Huang doesn't think AI is coming for your job. He thinks your coworker is.

"It is unlikely most people will lose a job to AI," Nvidia's CEO said at Stanford this month. "It is most likely that most people will lose their job to somebody who uses AI."

Huang is putting real money behind that belief. On the All-In Podcast at Nvidia's GTC conference in March, he described how AI coding tools like Cursor are now used pervasively across Nvidia's entire engineering organization to solve complex problems, arguing that increased AI productivity doesn't lead to layoffs but enables the company to do more work and explore a wider frontier of ideas.

He's not the only executive thinking this way. Meta CTO Andrew Bosworth has said his best engineer spends the equivalent of their entire salary on AI tokens and is five to 10 times more productive because of it. In one 30-day stretch, Meta employees collectively burned through more than 60 trillion tokens. The company even ran an internal leaderboard ranking its heaviest users as "Token Legend" and "Cache Wizard" before quietly pulling it down.

Huang's broader point, as he told Morgan Stanley: compute creates intelligence, intelligence creates a digital workforce, and that workforce creates revenue. Every company, he argues, will eventually need compute the way it currently needs headcount.

The career data is starting to back him up. Workers with demonstrated AI fluency now command a 56% wage premium over comparable workers who haven't adopted the tools. AI power users are roughly three times more likely to have received promotions and raises in the past year. As we reported Sunday, a new class of "AI elite" employees is already forming inside organizations, with executives basing career decisions on who's actually using the technology.

Most companies, though, aren't matching the expectation with support. Only 35% of organizations have mature, company-wide AI training programs, even as workers who receive structured training achieve proficiency 2.7 times higher than those left to figure it out alone.

Huang's take is actually moderate compared to some of his peers. Anthropic's Dario Amodei has predicted half of entry-level white-collar jobs could be displaced entirely. Nobel laureate Daron Acemoglu has called that kind of prediction "motivated reasoning," noting that AI companies keep forecasting massive disruption while building more of the technology they say causes it.

Into the Valley

Huang sells the chips that make all of this run, so take the framing accordingly. But the 56% wage premium is a labor market signal, not a marketing slide. AI fluency is quickly becoming the most important career skill that almost nobody is formally teaching. The companies that invest in closing that gap will pull ahead. Everyone else will keep mandating adoption, skipping the training, and watching their best people walk to the places that figured it out first.

title: DeepSeek V4 doesn't need Nvidia
subtitle: DeepSeek released V4, its most powerful model yet, optimized to run entirely on Huawei's Ascend chips instead of Nvidia hardware.
author: Thorium Valley
content:
On April 15, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang went on the Dwarkesh Podcast and warned that "the day that DeepSeek comes out on Huawei first, that is a horrible outcome for [the U.S.]."

That day came nine days later.

DeepSeek released V4 on Friday, its most powerful model yet, optimized to run entirely on Huawei's Ascend chips instead of Nvidia hardware. Huawei confirmed that its full Ascend supernode product line now supports the model. DeepSeek researcher Deli Chen posted on X that "AGI belongs to everyone," as the company released V4 under an open-source license. The whole point of US export controls was to prevent exactly this.

V4 isn't the best model in the world, and DeepSeek knows it. The company's own tech report admits it trails GPT-5.4 and Gemini 3.1 Pro by roughly three to six months. But on coding and reasoning tasks, V4 is close enough that the gap barely matters for most practical work, and it got there on hardware the US tried to keep out of China's hands.

Then there's the cost. V4-Pro charges $3.48 per million output tokens, while OpenAI charges $15 for GPT-5.4 and Anthropic charges $25 for Claude Opus 4.5. The lightweight V4-Flash model costs just $0.28. For most practical uses, the performance gap matters a lot less when the price gap is that extreme.

DeepSeek can charge that little because V4 was built from the ground up to do more with less. The model includes a new attention system that cuts compute by roughly 73% on long tasks, which partially compensates for Huawei's weaker chips. Huawei's rotating chairman Eric Xu acknowledged at MWC 2026 that the company trails Nvidia on a per-chip basis, but said the strategy is to "win at the cluster level" by networking thousands of cheaper chips together. DeepSeek's software is what makes that strategy viable.

It's not without tradeoffs. DeepSeek researcher Yuchen Jin noted that "the biggest challenge for Chinese chips is the stability of long-cycle training." Running thousands of weaker chips in tandem for weeks at a time is fragile in ways that Nvidia's hardware simply isn't. V4 is impressive precisely because it works despite those constraints.

Washington is paying attention. On the same day V4 launched, the State Department sent a diplomatic cable to allies warning that Chinese AI models "enable foreign actors to release products that appear to perform comparably on select benchmarks at a fraction of the cost."

Earlier this year, the Commerce Department revised its export policy to allow case-by-case review of advanced Nvidia and AMD chip sales to China. Jeffrey Kessler, Under Secretary for Industry and Security, said the intent was for "export controls to evolve with changes in technology."

But even when Chinese companies received approval to buy Nvidia chips, the restrictions were reportedly so cumbersome that no orders actually went through, pushing more labs toward domestic alternatives. Lian Jye Su, chief analyst at tech research firm Omdia, told Reuters that DeepSeek's domestic popularity drove the company to optimize for Huawei hardware in the first place, which in turn "lowers the barriers for Chinese developers and companies" to build entirely on Chinese chips. Huang warned on that same podcast that if AI models get increasingly optimized around a non-American tech stack, Chinese standards could become the global default.

Into the Valley

Three to six months behind the frontier, on worse hardware, at a tenth of the price. If that gap keeps narrowing, export controls won't just have failed to prevent competitive Chinese AI. They'll have accidentally created a more efficient competitor that American labs had no incentive to become. The next few model generations will tell us whether V4 is an outlier or the start of a pattern where the most efficient lab, not the best-funded one, sets the pace.

title: AI is eating the world's memory chips
subtitle: For the first time ever, memory chip orders have surpassed logic chips at ASML — almost entirely because of AI.
author: Thorium Valley
content:
AI is consuming so much of the world's memory chip supply that there isn't enough left for everyone else.

For the first time ever, orders for memory chips have surpassed orders for logic chips at ASML, the Dutch company that builds the machines chipmakers need to manufacture advanced semiconductors. Logic chips are the processors that run your phone and laptop. Memory chips store and move data. Processors were always the bigger business, until AI changed the equation.

AI data centers require massive amounts of a specialized memory called HBM (High Bandwidth Memory) to function, and chipmakers are scrambling to meet that demand. The tradeoff is zero-sum: every wafer dedicated to HBM is a wafer not making the conventional memory that goes into your phone, laptop, or car.

Micron, one of three companies that dominate global memory production, reported record revenue of $13.6 billion last quarter, up 57% year over year. DRAM prices alone jumped 20% in a single quarter. The company has already sold out its entire 2026 HBM supply and is guiding next quarter for 68% gross margins, almost unheard of for what's always been a commodity business.

Even with all of that, Micron still can't keep up. "Despite significant efforts, we are disappointed to be unable to meet demand from our customers, across all market segments," the company said in its earnings call prepared remarks.

TSMC CEO C.C. Wei confirmed how deep the demand runs on his latest earnings call: "AI is so strong... Our customers, and customers of customers, who are mainly the cloud service providers, continue to provide us with their very strong signal and positive outlook."

The shortage is now cascading into consumer markets:

  • IDC's Francisco Jeronimo called it a "tsunami-like shock originating in the memory supply chain."
  • Gartner's Ranjit Atwal warned of "the steepest contraction in device shipments in over a decade," with higher prices pushing consumers to hold onto their phones and laptops longer.

It's also reaching industries you wouldn't think of. Ford CFO Sherry House recently acknowledged that while the automaker has enough memory chips for now, the company is already building pricing pressure into forward plans. Modern vehicles rely on memory for everything from infotainment to driver-assist systems, and if those prices keep climbing, that shows up on the window sticker.

Micron forecasts the HBM market alone will grow from roughly $35 billion in 2025 to around $100 billion by 2028. That single product category will be larger than the entire DRAM market was in 2024. And even with Micron increasing capital expenditures to $20 billion this year, most of that increase is going toward HBM, not conventional memory.

Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan summed up the timeline: "There's no relief until 2028."

Into the Valley

Previous chip shortages were caused by supply disruptions like COVID shutdowns and natural disasters, which meant they corrected once production came back online. This one is demand-driven, and the companies buying HBM aren't planning to slow down. Every new model release, every new data center, every new agent framework makes the hunger worse. Your next phone, your next laptop, and possibly your next car are going to cost more because AI needs the same memory they do, and right now AI is first in line. 2028 feels optimistic.

title: The C-suite can't agree on who owns AI
subtitle: Nearly 43% of Fortune 500 companies have a Chief AI Officer. The average one lasts 2.1 years.
author: Thorium Valley
content:
Everybody wants to lead the AI strategy. Owning the results is a different conversation.

Nearly 43% of Fortune 500 companies now have a Chief AI Officer or equivalent, up from about 19% a year ago. That's a massive hiring wave. The problem is that the average CAIO lasts about 2.1 years in the job, roughly half the tenure of a typical CTO or CFO. Companies are creating the role faster than they can figure out what it's supposed to do.

The deeper issue is pretty simple. AI touches everything, so every executive thinks it belongs under their umbrella. The CTO sees it as a technology decision. The CFO sees it as a spending question. The COO treats it as an operations issue. When everyone claims ownership, the work between them falls through the cracks.

One executive at a Melbourne-based financial services firm described the fallout: "We had 17 different AI projects running across seven departments. Nobody knew what anyone else was doing. We had three teams independently building similar solutions."

That kind of duplication is costing real money. Organizations without centralized AI governance spend 40% more on AI initiatives while getting 30% less value out of them.

Hiring a CAIO doesn't automatically fix it, either, because there's no agreement on where the role even sits. 54% of Fortune 500 CAIOs report to the CEO, 31% to the CTO, and 15% to a COO or CDO. Each reporting line creates a fundamentally different version of the job.

The companies figuring this out aren't relying on a single title. They're building cross-functional governance councils:

  • Microsoft stood up overlapping governance bodies across its internal digital team. Don Campbell, Senior Director of Employee Experience Success, said the company specifically avoided implementing AI for its own sake and instead tied every project to measurable business outcomes.
  • Dow Jones created a steering committee that gives departments visibility into what everyone else is building. Ingrid Verschuren, EVP of Data and AI, told Digiday the setup prevents redundant work by directing teams to existing solutions before they start from scratch.
  • Intermountain Health uses governance as a filter. Ryan Smith, the health system's Chief Digital and Information Officer, said his team turns down most AI proposals. "We say 'no' to an awful lot of AI," Smith said, though the system has still deployed over 300 AI tools into production. In healthcare, being selective isn't caution. It's the strategy.

Then there's the finding that challenges the entire CAIO premise. Only 2% of companies give AI value accountability to the CFO. But when they do, 76% achieve significant value, compared to just 53% under CIO or CTO oversight, according to Fortune. DBS Bank, which has its unit CFOs vet AI value numbers before they get rolled up to leadership, reports roughly million in economic value from its data and AI programs.

CFOs are trained to kill underperforming projects, track returns, and hold people accountable to numbers. Those are exactly the muscles most AI strategies are missing.

Into the Valley

The CAIO hiring wave looks a lot like the "Chief Digital Officer" wave from a decade ago, where companies created a new role to signal they took something seriously without changing how decisions actually got made. Most CDO roles eventually got absorbed or quietly disappeared. AI governance will probably follow a similar path, not because the problem isn't real, but because the fix isn't another title. It's forcing the people already at the table to agree on who answers for it when an initiative burns money and goes nowhere. That's a much harder conversation than posting a job listing.

title: SpaceX bets $60 billion on AI coding
subtitle: SpaceX wants to pay $60 billion for a coding assistant. The tool's flagship model runs on a Chinese base model.
author: Thorium Valley
content:
SpaceX wants to pay $60 billion for a coding assistant.

On Tuesday, SpaceX announced a deal with Cursor, the AI-powered coding tool used by over 50,000 engineering teams at companies like Nvidia, Uber, and Salesforce. SpaceX can either pay $10 billion for a dedicated partnership or acquire the entire company for $60 billion later this year. No competing bids allowed while the deal is open.

That price values Cursor at roughly 30 times its $2 billion in annual recurring revenue. Typical SaaS companies trade at 8 to 15 times. Cursor was worth $2.5 billion in January 2025 and has jumped 24x since, fueled by enterprise customers that now make up 60% of revenue and a forecast of $6 billion ARR by year's end.

In January, Anthropic cut off xAI's access to Claude models after discovering xAI was using Cursor to help train competing AI systems. Anthropic had done the same to OpenAI months earlier for a similar violation. For SpaceX, which absorbed xAI in February, losing access to a foundational model provider made owning a coding tool feel a lot more urgent.

Martin Casado, an Andreessen Horowitz general partner and Cursor board member, called Cursor "the fastest-growing company we've ever seen" if you subtract out the dollars invested. He also has a financial interest in that being true.

Jerry Murdock, co-founder of Insight Partners, said on the 20VC podcast that "most of the companies I mentioned... their view is that Cursor is obsolete today." There's data to back that up. Claude Code overtook Cursor in primary-tool market share for the first time in Q1 2026, hitting 28% versus Cursor's 24%, while GitHub Copilot still leads the paid market at 42%. As we reported Thursday, OpenAI's Codex is also expanding rapidly beyond coding, with 3 million weekly users and 70% month-over-month growth.

Cursor's Composer, its flagship agentic coding model, is fine-tuned on Kimi 2.5, a Chinese base model built by Moonshot AI. SpaceX builds rockets for the Pentagon. Gartner principal analyst Nitish Tyagi has flagged the Chinese model dependency as a security concern, and IDC's Deepika Giri warned that Cursor's zero-data-retention agreements with providers like OpenAI and Anthropic "could be challenged under the new SpaceX ownership."

Into the Valley

The $60 billion gets all the attention, but SpaceX quietly left itself a $10 billion exit ramp. The deal lets SpaceX pay that amount for the partnership and walk away from the acquisition entirely. With Claude Code and Codex both gaining ground and Cursor's core model built on Chinese infrastructure a Pentagon contractor shouldn't be running, that exit clause could prove to be the smartest part of the whole deal.

That price values Cursor at roughly 30 times its $2 billion in annual recurring revenue — typical SaaS companies trade at 8 to 15 times. The urgency has a backstory. In January, Anthropic cut off xAI's access to Claude models after discovering xAI was using Cursor to help train competing AI systems. For SpaceX, which absorbed xAI in February, losing access to a foundational model provider made owning a coding tool feel a lot more urgent.

But Cursor's dominance is no longer guaranteed. Claude Code overtook it in primary-tool market share for the first time in Q1 2026, hitting 28% versus Cursor's 24%. GitHub Copilot still leads the paid market at 42%. And as we reported Thursday, OpenAI's Codex is expanding rapidly beyond coding, with 3 million weekly users and 70% month-over-month growth.

There's also a geopolitical wrinkle. Cursor's flagship agentic model, Composer, is fine-tuned on Kimi 2.5, a Chinese base model built by Moonshot AI. SpaceX builds rockets for the Pentagon. A Chinese model dependency inside a defense contractor's core tooling is exactly the kind of thing that draws scrutiny — and it raises real questions about whether the deal survives as structured.

The $60 billion gets all the attention, but SpaceX quietly left itself a $10 billion exit ramp. With Claude Code and Codex both gaining ground and Cursor's core model built on Chinese infrastructure a Pentagon contractor shouldn't be running, that escape clause could prove to be the smartest part of the whole deal.

title: Bezos bets $10 billion on physical AI
subtitle: The biggest AI raise of the year doesn't involve a chatbot. It involves robots.
author: Thorium Valley
content:
The biggest AI raise of the year doesn't involve a chatbot.

Jeff Bezos' venture, Project Prometheus, is close to raising $10 billion at a $38 billion valuation, with BlackRock and JPMorgan among the backers. The lab is focused on physical AI: building machines that can see, move and make decisions in the real world rather than generate text on a screen.

Up to this point, the AI boom has mostly been about language: chatbots, coding assistants, search engines. Physical AI is the bet that the bigger payoff is in machines that actually do things, whether that's robots on factory floors, autonomous warehouse systems or vehicles that drive themselves. Bezos, who built Amazon's logistics empire from scratch, is betting that AI's most valuable applications won't be digital.

The valuation is what jumps out. Figure AI, which actually builds and ships humanoid robots, recently closed over $1 billion in Series C funding at a nearly identical $39 billion valuation. Figure already has a production line capable of building up to 12,000 robots a year, with a goal of 100,000 over the next four. Apptronik raised $935 million for its own humanoid robotics work. Prometheus raised more than both of them combined and doesn't appear to have revenue yet.

Bezos isn't putting all his chips on Prometheus, either. Through Bezos Expeditions, he also invested in Skild AI, a robotics company that raised $1.4 billion at a valuation over $14 billion. Unlike Prometheus, Skild has paying customers, having grown from zero to about $30 million in revenue within months across security, construction and warehouse deployments. It's a portfolio play: fund the moonshot and the company already making money, then see which one takes off.

Bezos isn't the only one making this bet. NVIDIA partnered with Siemens to build AI-driven manufacturing sites, with the first going live in Germany this year and companies like Foxconn, HD Hyundai and PepsiCo already evaluating the technology. Jensen Huang called physical AI "the next frontier of artificial intelligence" at an industry event earlier this year.

The skeptics have a case, though. Bessemer Venture Partners described the current moment in robotics as "the GPT-2.5 moment," meaning the demos look real but reliable deployment at scale hasn't arrived. There are also hard infrastructure constraints: more than 200 gigawatts of energy projects are stuck in U.S. interconnection queues, bottlenecking the very facilities this buildout depends on.

Into the Valley

The most telling detail isn't the $10 billion, it's that a pre-revenue lab and a company with an actual robot factory are valued within a billion dollars of each other. Investors aren't pricing what physical AI can do today. They're pricing where they think it'll be in five years, and that kind of forward pricing has defined both tech's greatest wins and its worst flameouts. Bezos seems to know this, which is why he's not picking one winner. He's funding his own lab and backing competitors at the same time, so whichever version of physical AI wins, he has a stake in it.

title: OpenAI's $2 billion a month still isn't enough
subtitle: OpenAI brings in $2 billion a month in revenue. It's still not close to breaking even.
author: Thorium Valley
content:
OpenAI brings in $2 billion a month in revenue. It's still not close to breaking even.

The company said it now has 900 million weekly active users, over 50 million paying subscribers, and an enterprise business that accounts for more than 40% of revenue. It recently closed $122 billion in funding at an $852 billion valuation, the largest private fundraise in history. By any normal startup measure, OpenAI is a juggernaut.

The spending tells a different story. HSBC analysts project OpenAI's total infrastructure costs will hit roughly $792 billion through 2030, with a cumulative funding gap of about $207 billion even after expected revenue. If OpenAI doubles its number of paying users, the gap only drops by half.

Those costs come from infrastructure deals that keep getting bigger. The company just signed a $50 billion partnership with Amazon that expands an existing AWS agreement by $100 billion over eight years and commits OpenAI to consuming 2 gigawatts of power. That's layered on top of existing arrangements with Microsoft, Oracle, CoreWeave, Google Cloud, and custom chip deals with NVIDIA and Broadcom. "No startup in history has operated with losses on anything approaching this scale," Deutsche Bank analysts wrote in a recent report.

OpenAI's backers say the math works if you give it time. Ethan Choi, an OpenAI investor at Khosla Ventures, has argued that most of the infrastructure costs will be shouldered by partners building the actual data centers, and that OpenAI's projected compute capacity could eventually generate $140 billion a year in revenue.

Not everyone is willing to wait. Some of OpenAI's own investors are hedging by writing larger checks to Anthropic. Roy Luo, a partner at Iconiq Capital, which put over $1 billion into Anthropic while holding a smaller OpenAI stake, told the Financial Times: "There's room for both, but there is fundamentally a number one and a number two dynamic, and the number one will win disproportionately. We picked."

Anthropic is an easy alternative to get excited about. The company has reportedly turned down funding offers valuing it above $800 billion, hasn't made anywhere near the same infrastructure commitments, and is growing enterprise revenue fast. Where OpenAI needs the AI revolution to arrive on schedule, Anthropic is running leaner and letting the revenue catch up.

The pressure is showing internally, too. OpenAI's CFO Sarah Friar has reportedly told colleagues she doesn't believe the company will be ready for an IPO in 2026, citing spending risks and organizational gaps. When investor Brad Gerstner pressed Altman last fall on how a company generating $13 billion a year could commit to $1.4 trillion in total spending, Altman was blunt: "If you want to sell your shares, I'll find you a buyer. Enough."

Into the Valley

Altman has said openly that the AI industry will see booms and busts. The problem is that $792 billion in infrastructure commitments don't pause for a bust. If revenue scales the way OpenAI projects, this goes down as the boldest bet in tech history. If it takes even a couple years longer than planned, the math starts to break. The investors quietly moving money toward Anthropic aren't betting against OpenAI so much as betting that the company willing to spend less might be the one still standing when the correction Altman himself is predicting finally shows up.

title: The math behind why AI agents keep failing
subtitle: Multiply 90% accuracy across ten steps and you land at 35%. Most companies plan to deploy them anyway.
author: Thorium Valley
content:
AI agents are supposed to handle your work while you sleep. The problem is they can barely handle it while you watch.

Close to three-quarters of companies plan to deploy agentic AI within two years, according to Deloitte's latest State of AI report. But only 25% have managed to move even 40% of their AI pilots into full production. The gap between what companies want agents to do and what agents can actually pull off has a surprisingly straightforward explanation: basic multiplication.

When you ask AI to do one thing, like summarize a document or draft an email, it works well. Single-step tasks succeed 90% of the time or better. But agents aren't built to do one thing. They're built to chain tasks together: read this spreadsheet, spot the trends, build a presentation, send it to your team.

Each step in that chain carries its own failure rate, and those rates compound. If every step works 90% of the time, a five-step workflow succeeds about 59% of the time. A ten-step workflow? Roughly 35%. The longer the chain, the more likely something breaks.

This shows up clearly in practice. A developer using Anthropic's Claude Dispatch reported a roughly 50% success rate on anything beyond simple operations. Basic file tasks worked fine. The moment you asked for a real multi-step workflow, like analyzing a CSV, pulling out trends and building a presentation around them, it was a coin flip. Benchmarks on real-world industrial tasks found similar results: no model broke 70% on single tasks, and when researchers added a planning step where the AI maps out what to do before doing it, success rates dropped from 65% to 38% for the best performer.

What makes this harder to fix is that raw accuracy isn't even the right thing to measure. Researcher Guy Freeman ran a comparison between a standard AI agent and a simpler system designed to understand the cost of being wrong:

  • The standard agent got more answers right at 63.7% accuracy but scored negative points overall because it confidently charged through every question, including ones it should have skipped.
  • The simpler system had lower raw accuracy at 59.6% but outscored the standard agent by 120 points because it knew when to stop.

Freeman then tried fixing the standard agent with better prompting, telling it to be more cost-conscious and careful. It scored even worse. "The word 'agent' in 'agentic AI' is doing an enormous amount of work whilst meaning almost nothing," he wrote. "What it actually describes is a language model with a for-loop."

None of this is slowing companies down. Deloitte found that 85% of organizations plan to customize agents for their specific needs, but only 21% have mature governance for how those agents should operate. And 37% are still using AI at a surface level with no real changes to their underlying workflows, essentially bolting agents onto processes that weren't designed for them.

Companies that do go all-in are seeing results. A Grant Thornton survey found that organizations with fully integrated AI were nearly four times as likely to report revenue growth compared to those still running pilots, 58% versus 15%. But those organizations are far from the norm. Most are stuck between deploying agents and getting them to actually deliver, and the compounding math of multi-step failure is the wall in between.

Into the Valley

The agent pitch has always been built on demos where every step works perfectly in sequence. Real work is not a demo. The companies that get the most out of agents in the near term won't be the ones handing over ten-step workflows and hoping for the best. They'll be the ones who understand that 90% reliability per step is a coin flip by step ten, and build their processes around that reality. Until the models get meaningfully better at sustained, autonomous execution, the smartest play is a shorter leash, not a longer one.

title: Apple and Meta are making opposite bets on AI glasses
subtitle: Meta's glasses sales tripled. Apple hasn't shipped a pair. Both think they'll win.
author: Thorium Valley
content:
Meta's glasses sales tripled last year. Apple hasn't shipped a single pair. Both companies think they're going to win.

On the Meta side, the numbers are hard to argue with. Mark Zuckerberg called Ray-Ban Meta glasses "some of the fastest growing consumer electronics in history" during Q4 earnings, and Meta captured 72.2% of the XR market in 2025 as the overall category grew 44.4%. In September, it launched the Ray-Ban Display at $799 — its first glasses with an actual screen — paired with an EMG wristband that reads muscle signals so you can control things without touching anything. EssilorLuxottica is expanding the lineup further with two new prescription-ready models at $499.

Zuckerberg's vision is clear: "Glasses are going to be able to see what you see, hear what you hear, talk to you and help you as you go about your day." Meanwhile, Meta Quest headset shipments fell 42.3% last year — the company is going all-in on faces, not foreheads.

Apple is playing a completely different game. Leaked designs reported by MacRumors suggest glasses that look like regular glasses — no display, heavy emphasis on design. That lines up with what we previously reported: Apple is prioritizing cameras and audio over screens, leaning on Siri and its Gemini integration for the intelligence layer.

The strategic divergence is real:

  • Meta is building an AI-first face computer. Cameras on, always listening, feeding everything to Meta AI. The glasses are the product.
  • Apple appears to be building a fashion accessory that happens to have AI capabilities, with privacy as the selling point rather than an afterthought.

And privacy is exactly where Meta's strategy gets complicated. Earlier this year, whistleblowers revealed that Meta had been harvesting Ray-Ban user videos and sending them to human contractors for AI training, including sensitive content recorded accidentally. The company also internally developed a facial recognition feature called "Name Tag" that would identify people in real time. As these devices get more capable and more people wear them in public, that's a liability waiting to grow.

Here's what's interesting: display-less smart glasses already represent the majority of XR shipments, and display-enabled glasses aren't expected to outsell VR/MR headsets until 2027. Apple's no-display bet aligns with where the market is right now. Meta's display push is a bet on where it's going. Both could be right — just on different timelines.

Our Valley View

Meta has the numbers, the distribution, and the momentum. Apple has none of the market share, but it has something Meta has struggled to earn: the benefit of the doubt on privacy. The question is whether Apple can ship something compelling before Meta's lead becomes insurmountable. If the Siri overhaul keeps slipping and Apple's glasses arrive without a credible AI experience behind them, all the privacy goodwill in the world won't close the gap. Meta learned from putting too much tech on people's faces with VR headsets. Apple's risk is putting too little.

title: ChatGPT ads hit $100M. Brands aren't biting.
subtitle: OpenAI crossed $100M in ad revenue in six weeks — but click-through rates are seven times below Google.
author: Thorium Valley
content:
OpenAI crossed $100 million in ChatGPT ad revenue in just six weeks. Impressive — until you look at the performance.

Since launching ads for free and low-cost tier users, OpenAI has signed more than 600 advertisers. But the clicks aren't following. An Adthena analysis of 29 million queries found ChatGPT ads averaging a 0.91% click-through rate — Google Search pulls 6.4% in the same categories. The pricing gap is just as stark:

  • CPM: ChatGPT charges roughly $60 CPM, about three times Meta's average and well above Google Search.
  • Minimum buy-in: Early pilot access required $200,000, though that reportedly dropped to $50,000 in April.
  • Spend problems: One enterprise advertiser in the early pilot burned just 3% of a $250,000 budget over several weeks because the platform couldn't deliver enough impressions to spend the rest.

OpenAI has framed the ads as a way to keep ChatGPT accessible, not as a revenue play, and says ads never influence the chatbot's answers. Anthropic, meanwhile, has argued that advertising fundamentally doesn't belong in AI conversations.

Our Valley View

The $100M headline sounds like validation, but click-through rates seven times lower than Google and advertisers who literally can't spend their budgets tell a different story. This looks less like the foundation of an ad business and more like brands paying a premium to be early — ahead of OpenAI's planned IPO later this year. The real test isn't whether advertisers show up. It's whether they renew once the performance data settles.

title: Nearly one in three workers admit to sabotaging company AI
subtitle: 29% of employees are deliberately undermining AI mandates. Gen Z leads at 44%.
author: Thorium Valley
content:
Companies keep mandating AI adoption. Nearly a third of workers are responding by sabotaging it.

A survey from Workplace Intelligence and enterprise AI platform Writer (which has a commercial interest here, but the findings track with broader trends) found that 29% of employees admit to deliberately undermining their company's AI strategy — feeding data into unapproved tools, using unsanctioned apps, or flat-out refusing to use what they've been told to adopt. Gen Z leads at 44%.

The threats behind these mandates are real: 60% of companies plan to lay off employees who won't adopt AI, and 77% won't consider non-proficient workers for promotions. But the strategy driving those threats? Leadership doesn't even believe in it.

According to Writer's enterprise AI report:

  • 75% of executives say their company's AI strategy is "more for show" than real guidance
  • Nearly half call the entire effort a "massive disappointment," up from 34% last year
  • 69% of companies are planning AI-related layoffs — while 39% lack a formal strategy to make money from the tools in the first place

So workers are being threatened with termination over a strategy their own bosses admit is performative. And as HR Dive reported, those broad AI goals from leadership rarely translate into actual guidance on the ground — leaving workers to guess, hit one bad experience, and revert to old routines.

Rather than rethinking the rollout, most companies are doubling down on the workers who already get it. The survey found that 92% of C-suite executives are cultivating a class of "AI elite" employees who are roughly three times more likely to have been promoted. The gap between super-users and everyone else is widening fast.

Our Valley View

You can't threaten people into using tools they don't understand under a strategy the C-suite itself calls performative and expect anything other than resentment. The companies that get real returns from AI will be the ones that treat it as a collaboration problem, not a compliance one — with genuine training and an honest answer to the question nobody at the top seems willing to ask: what exactly are we trying to do with this?

title: AI is making everyone's work look the same
subtitle: Duke researchers found every major AI model aces creativity tests — but they all ace them the exact same way.
author: Thorium Valley
content:
Every major AI model can ace a creativity test on its own. They also all ace it the same way.

Researchers at Duke University and the Technion–Israel Institute of Technology tested 22 large language models, including offerings from OpenAI, Google, Meta and Mistral, on three standardized creativity tests alongside 102 human participants.

Each model individually scored as well as or slightly better than the average human. But when the researchers compared AI outputs to each other, the picture changed. AI responses were far more similar to one another than human responses were, across every test.

The gap wasn't subtle. On one measure, the effect size hit 2.2, nearly three times what social scientists consider "large." Emily Wenger, one of the study's authors and a professor of electrical and computer engineering at Duke, said she wanted to investigate whether this homogenization phenomenon would occur in commercial LLMs and what the implications might be.

The reason is pretty straightforward. Every major commercial model has been trained on essentially the same data (the internet) and optimized for the same objective. Companies that lean hardest on AI for creative work are quietly erasing the thing that made them different. Every major model trains on the same internet and optimizes for the same goals, so the more teams rely on them without adding something of their own, the more everything blends together. AI was supposed to democratize creativity. It might just be standardizing it.

title: Gen Z won't quit AI, but the enthusiasm is gone
subtitle: A Gallup survey found Gen Z uses AI just as much but likes it 14 points less — even daily users are souring.
author: Thorium Valley
content:
Gen Z uses AI just as much as last year. They like it a lot less.

A Gallup survey commissioned by the Walton Family Foundation found that 51% of Gen Zers (ages 14 to 29) use generative AI at least weekly, a rate basically unchanged from March 2025. But excitement about AI dropped 14 percentage points over the past year, falling to just 22%. Anger surged 9 points to 31%. Anxiety held steady at 42%.

That shift isn't limited to people who barely use it, either. Among Gen Zers who use AI every single day, excitement still fell 18 points year over year. That breaks the usual pattern for technology adoption, where the more people use something, the more they tend to like it. Gen Z is doing the opposite.

Gallup senior researcher Zach Hrynowski noted the oldest Zoomers are the most skeptical because they're "acutely aware" of AI's power to reshape their world without a second thought. The workforce data backs him up: 48% of employed Gen Zers now say AI's risks outweigh its benefits, up from 37% a year ago.

Their concerns go deeper than losing a job. Gen Z is making pointed judgments about what AI does to the way they think:

  • Critical thinking: 42% say AI is harmful to their ability to think carefully about information, versus 25% who call it helpful.
  • Creativity: 38% say AI hurts their ability to come up with new ideas on their own.
  • Learning: 80% believe using AI tools will make it harder for them to learn in the future.

That skepticism is already showing up at work. Kevin Chung, Chief Strategy Officer at Writer, noted in Writer's 2025 Enterprise AI Adoption Report that two years ago, nine out of 10 employee complaints were about displacement: "Why am I training the robot that's going to take my job?" Today, that specific fear has faded, but the resistance hasn't. Instead, he sees employees actively ignoring AI tools or quietly working around them because they don't believe in the strategy behind them.

It doesn't help that tech leaders keep raising the temperature. Anthropic's Dario Amodei has warned AI could eliminate half of entry-level white-collar jobs. Microsoft's Mustafa Suleyman has suggested all white-collar work could eventually be automated. For a generation watching the ground shift beneath them, those kinds of statements feel more like threats than forecasts.

"Employers are making room for AI investments," researcher Alex Hanna told Fortune. "They want to show that they can lay off people and do what they're currently doing with a decrease in headcount."

Our Valley View

The tech industry assumed Gen Z would adopt AI like they adopted everything else: fast and with minimal friction. What the Gallup data shows is a generation fluent enough in technology to see exactly what AI threatens, and they're watching it reshape a job market they haven't fully entered yet. Companies building their AI strategies around the idea that younger workers will naturally lead adoption might want to check whether that assumption still holds. The workers who grew up on the internet aren't afraid of new technology. They're just not convinced this particular technology is on their side.

title: A robot just outran every human alive
subtitle: Honor's robot finished the Beijing Half Marathon in under 51 minutes — nearly seven minutes faster than the human world record.
author: Thorium Valley
content:
Last weekend at the Beijing Half Marathon, Honor's "Lightning" robot finished the 21-kilometer course in 50 minutes and 26 seconds. That's nearly seven minutes faster than the human world record.

The robot ran the full course autonomously, with no remote control and no human operator steering it. It was one of roughly 300 humanoid robots from 26 brands that lined up alongside human runners in what's quietly become the most revealing annual showcase for the robotics industry.

A year ago, the winning time in the race's inaugural edition was 2 hours and 40 minutes. This year, it dropped to under 51. Robots got nearly two-thirds faster in 12 months.

"It's the first time robots have surpassed humans, and that's something I never imagined," said Sun Zhigang, a spectator who attended the race with his son.

It wasn't exactly graceful. One robot fell at the starting line. Another struck a barrier mid-course. About 60% of the 102 teams relied on remote control rather than full autonomy. A German team showed up with their robot in running shoes.

But the spectacle, which also included a viral clip of a humanoid chasing wild boars through Warsaw the same week, is overshadowing a more significant shift. The money pouring into humanoid robotics has started to look less like VC enthusiasm and more like early-stage industrialization:

  • Apptronik closed a $520 million extension to bring its total Series A to $935 million, one of the largest early-stage robotics rounds ever.
  • Figure raised over $1 billion in its Series C at a $39 billion valuation.
  • AGIBOT, a Chinese robotics company, was ranked No. 1 worldwide in humanoid robot shipments for 2025 by research firm Omdia.
  • Siemens completed a proof of concept with startup Humanoid to test robots in industrial logistics at its factory in Erlangen, Germany.

China is pushing especially hard. The government published a five-year blueprint to fast-track humanoid robot adoption in manufacturing, and dozens of Chinese firms are racing to move from lab demos to commercial deployments. Liu Qing, director of the Yangtze River Delta National Innovation Center, described the path in stages: lab R&D gets you from "0 to 1," pilot testing takes you from "1 to 10," and enterprises are responsible for scaling "10 into thousands and millions." Most of the industry is still somewhere between zero and one.

The gap between finishing a half marathon and doing useful work remains enormous. Battery life still tops out at two to three hours per charge. Cutting-edge research models cost millions of dollars, and commercial versions need to come down to roughly $42,000 before enterprises see a reasonable return on investment. And tasks that feel instinctive to people, like gripping an oddly shaped object, can still trip up machines because a rigid robotic finger is simply in the wrong place.

Wang Xingxing, founder and CEO of Unitree Robotics, has a clear benchmark for when the industry has truly arrived: "A true 'ChatGPT moment' for the sector will come when robots, placed in unfamiliar real-world settings, can complete about 80 percent of tasks simply by following voice or text instructions."

Our Valley View

A year ago, the fastest robot in Beijing needed nearly three hours to finish a half marathon. Now one can beat the human world record. That kind of improvement doesn't happen in a field that's stalling out, and the billions flowing in suggest investors agree. The question is whether the factory floor catches up to the racetrack before the hype cycle turns, because right now, the robots are running faster than the business model.

title: AI saves hours, until you count the rework
subtitle: Stanford researchers coined a word for the flood of low-quality AI output employees are expected to clean up.
author: Thorium Valley
content:
AI was supposed to save time at work. Stanford researchers have a word for what it's actually producing: "workslop."

The term, coined by a team of researchers including Jeff Hancock, describes the flood of low-quality AI-generated content that workers are now expected to review, fix and redo. Companies mandate the tools, celebrate the efficiency gains, then leave employees to clean up the output.

The most rigorous evidence that those gains aren't real comes from Denmark. A study published by the National Bureau of Economic Research linked AI adoption surveys to actual government payroll records and found essentially zero impact on earnings or hours worked. This wasn't a vibes-based survey. Researchers used administrative data precise enough to detect a 2% shift. They found nothing.

Workers in AI-exposed roles are adopting the tools and say they feel more productive. But those feelings aren't showing up in the economic data. "Technological change reshapes work well before it surfaces in earnings or hours," the researchers wrote. The work is changing shape. The paychecks are not.

New research from Workday shows where the time actually goes:

  • 85% of employees report saving one to seven hours a week with AI
  • Nearly 40% of that saved time gets lost to fixing low-quality AI output
  • 32% of companies respond to efficiency gains by simply increasing workloads

AI gives you an hour. Rework takes back 24 minutes. Your employer takes the rest.

A copywriter at a Miami cybersecurity firm described what happened after his company rolled out mandatory AI tools. "Quality decreased significantly, time to produce a piece of content increased significantly and, most importantly, morale decreased," he told The Guardian under a pseudonym. "Everything got a whole lot worse."

It's not just office workers. Philip Barrison, a University of Michigan researcher embedded in primary care clinics, told The Guardian that once doctors get past the novelty of AI tools, they tend to just tune them out. And Vivi Mengjie Xiao, a product manager in China who built six AI "employees" using OpenClaw, told Business Insider she's somehow working more than ever: "When your efficiency goes up, you don't work less. You just attempt more."

Aiha Nguyen, who runs the Labor Futures program at Data & Society, points to a structural problem: AI is being sold as a general-purpose tool that can handle anything, but it doesn't work that way. The gap between promise and reality generates its own category of busywork. That pattern might help explain why MIT NANDA researchers found that 95% of enterprise AI initiatives deliver zero measurable P&L impact.

The pitch for AI at work has always been save time, do more. What's actually happening is closer to do the same, plus fix what the machine got wrong. Companies are measuring success by adoption rates, not by whether the work actually gets better. Until that flips, the gap between the executive slide deck and an employee's actual Tuesday is only going to grow. "Workslop" exists because the experience needed a name.

title: The Pentagon tried to kill Anthropic. Revenue tripled.
subtitle: Anthropic refused mass surveillance and autonomous weapons. Two months later its revenue passed OpenAI's.
author: Thorium Valley
content:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth wanted to make an example of Anthropic. Two months later, the company's revenue reportedly passed OpenAI's.

In late February, the Pentagon threatened to designate Anthropic a "supply chain risk" and force military contractors to drop the company entirely. Anthropic was willing to work with the Defense Department on classified systems, but wouldn't sign off on mass surveillance of American citizens or autonomous weapons that can kill without a human in the loop.

In a February 27 statement, the company was blunt: "No amount of intimidation or punishment from the Department of War will change our position on mass domestic surveillance or fully autonomous weapons."

CEO Dario Amodei pointed out that the government's own threats didn't hold together. One arm of the Pentagon was calling Claude a security risk while another was calling it essential to national security. "These latter two threats are inherently contradictory," he wrote.

Steve Bannon, of all people, said Anthropic "had it right" in rejecting the deal. OpenAI, which signed its own agreement with the Defense Department, said it didn't understand why Anthropic "could not reach this deal." Outside analysts noted that OpenAI's agreement left key autonomous weapons concerns unresolved.

Users picked a side, too. ChatGPT uninstalls surged 295% the weekend after the news broke, while Claude hit No. 1 on the U.S. App Store.

Anthropic's revenue run rate was $14 billion in mid-February, already growing tenfold annually. By April, multiple industry trackers reported it had climbed to roughly $30 billion, reportedly surpassing OpenAI. The company closed a $30 billion Series G at a $380 billion valuation and has attracted investor interest at $800 billion. Axios called it growth with no precedent in American corporate history.

Anthropic also launched Project Glasswing, a cybersecurity initiative built around its unreleased Mythos model, assembling a coalition of more than 50 organizations including Apple, Google, Microsoft, Nvidia, CrowdStrike and Palo Alto Networks. Lee Klarich, Palo Alto Networks' Chief Product and Technology Officer, said his team used Mythos to "identify complex vulnerabilities that prior-generation models missed entirely." Anthropic's own Frontier Red Team says the model's capabilities aren't close to plateauing.

By mid-April, the White House appeared ready to come to the table. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chief of Staff Susie Wiles met with Amodei, and the administration is now reportedly considering giving federal agencies access to Claude Mythos.

Anthropic's defiance gave it something no marketing budget could buy: proof that it means what it says about safety. That credibility is now fueling an $800 billion valuation and partnerships with practically every major tech company. The real test comes when the financial pressure catches up. With tens of billions in investor capital expecting returns, the principled "no" gets harder to say each time, and the next standoff probably won't arrive with such clean optics. But refusing the most powerful institution on earth and watching your revenue explode is, at minimum, a hell of a business strategy.
